turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you. Could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, Dr. Smith, it is nice to meet you too. I suppose I am here because... well, my mind has just been so incredibly preoccupied lately with things at work. I am a secondary school teacher, you see, and I have been at my current school for quite some time, so I am very familiar with the daily routines, the administrative memos, the way the administration communicates, all of that. But recently, and this is what has been so distressing for me, I just can’t shake the feeling that certain staff emails and the morning announcements are actually coded messages about me. 

I know how that sounds, I really do, but when I sit at my desk during my planning period and open my inbox, the wording in these administrative updates... it just feels so incredibly specific to my life. Like there is a subtext there that I am supposed to be decoding, some hidden meaning about my performance or my personal life buried in a memo about, say, the new grading software or parking lot rules. 

And I have talked to my colleagues about it. They are very kind, they really are. A few of them have even sat down with me and gently shown me their own computers, pointing out that the emails were sent to the entire staff mailing list, or that the morning announcements over the loudspeaker are just general school business. They try to reassure me and prove that it is the exact same message everyone else is getting. But no matter how many times they show me their screens and prove that it was sent to everyone, I just cannot shake this deep, heavy feeling that the message is actually directed at me. It takes up so much of my mental energy, just analyzing every single word all day long, and I just... I really need some help figuring out why I cannot turn this feeling off.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient describes a fixed belief that general staff emails and announcements contain coded messages directed specifically at them, which persists even when colleagues provide contradictory evidence.

top_partial.disease_name: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features

turns.doctor_question: Aside from these thoughts about the emails and announcements, have you been experiencing any other unusual sensory experiences, such as hearing voices or seeing things that others do not seem to perceive?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it’s... it is interesting that you bring that up, because I have been very hesitant to mention it. It’s hard enough talking about the emails, but... yes, actually. I have been experiencing something else. 

You know how a high school is, Dr. Smith. During the day, it is just an absolute cacophony of noise—the bells ringing, lockers slamming, teenagers shouting down the hallways, the constant hum of the fluorescent lights. It's sensory overload, really. But then, after the final bell rings at 3:15, and the students finally clear out to go to soccer practice or catch the buses, there is this very specific kind of heavy, almost echoing silence that settles over my classroom. I usually stay late, you see, to grade papers or prep for the next day's lessons, just sitting at my desk by the window. And sometimes, when it is just completely quiet like that... or even later in the evening when I am finally back at my house, just doing something completely mundane like making a cup of chamomile tea in the kitchen or folding my laundry in the living room, I will hear... well, I hear a voice. 

It is a woman's voice. And it is so clear, just as crisp and clear as you sitting here talking to me right now. She will just say my name, just call out to me, or she might make a brief little comment about exactly what I am doing at that very moment. Just a short remark, like she's observing me. 

And the thing is, my immediate reaction is just completely reflexive. I will actually turn around and answer her! I'll say, "Yes?" or "Can I help you?" because I am so utterly convinced that one of the other teachers or maybe one of the evening custodians has walked into my room, or that someone has somehow gotten into my house. I answer her out loud, fully expecting someone to be standing right there. 

But then I look around, and... there is absolutely no one there. The room is completely empty. And I just stand there, holding a stack of history quizzes or my tea mug, feeling so... well, unsettled, because I know I heard it. I know I did. It’s not a whisper, it’s not the house settling or the wind outside, it’s a distinct woman's voice. And it just makes me wonder if I'm just so exhausted from analyzing all those administrative memos all day that my mind is... I don't know, it just happens when it's so quiet, and it really throws me off my rhythm when I'm just trying to get my grading done.

symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly describes hearing a clear woman's voice speaking to her when she is alone and no one else is present, which is a clear auditory hallucination.

Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features

turns.doctor_question: Aside from these experiences, have you noticed any significant, sustained changes in your mood—such as feeling profoundly low, hopeless, or unusually energetic and irritable—that have lasted for a week or more?
turns.patient_response:
Well, Dr. Smith, I... I don't think so. I really don't. I mean, of course, I get tired. Teaching high school is an incredibly demanding profession, as I am sure you can imagine. You are constantly "on," constantly having to project energy and enthusiasm, even when you are just completely drained. And with all of this... this business with the emails and the announcements, and then the voice in the quiet moments... it takes a toll. It really does. I feel exhausted by it all, and certainly frustrated, maybe a bit anxious about why I can't just brush it off like a normal person would. 

But as for feeling profoundly low or hopeless? No, I wouldn't say that. I still love my subject—I teach European History, by the way, which I have always been deeply passionate about. I still care very much about my students and whether they are grasping the material. I still look forward to my morning coffee and my weekend gardening. I haven't lost my zest for life, if that makes sense. I don't sit around crying or feeling like there's no point to anything. It's not a dark cloud of despair, it's just... a very specific, very heavy distraction.

And as for feeling unusually energetic or irritable... well, I am certainly not bouncing off the walls. I don't feel like I have a sudden surplus of energy, quite the opposite, really, given how much mental effort I am expending on decoding things. I suppose I might get a tiny bit short with my husband if he interrupts my train of thought while I'm trying to analyze an email from the principal, but it's not a sustained rage or anything like that. It's just normal annoyance. So no, no major mood swings that last for weeks on end. Just... just the exhaustion of dealing with everything else I've mentioned.

symptom_reasoning.S029: The patient explicitly states feeling tired and exhausted by their experiences and demanding job.
symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient explicitly denies feeling profoundly low or sitting around crying.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient denies losing their zest for life, noting they still love their subject and look forward to daily activities.
symptom_reasoning.S033: The patient denies feeling unusually irritable or having major mood swings, describing only normal, brief annoyance.
symptom_reasoning.S034: The patient denies having a sudden surplus of energy or bouncing off the walls.
symptom_reasoning.S083: The patient explicitly denies feeling hopeless or feeling like there is no point to anything.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed any changes in your ability to keep up with your daily personal hygiene or your usual household chores since these experiences began?
turns.patient_response:
Well, Dr. Smith, as far as the basic things like showering or keeping the kitchen clean... I mean, I still get up and shower and put on my professional attire every morning. You really have to when you're standing in front of thirty teenagers first thing in the morning; they notice absolutely everything, you know. And the laundry gets folded eventually, even if I'm a bit distracted while doing it. But... it is interesting that you ask about keeping up with things, because while the absolute bare minimum of my household chores gets done, the way I go about my life outside of the classroom has changed so profoundly. 

It’s hard to explain, but for many months now, it has just felt like... well, like the warmth and the drive have completely drained out of me. It's this deep, heavy lack of energy in my routine. I still care about my students, of course, and I care deeply about my friends, I truly do. But actually engaging with my life? That is a completely different story. 

I used to be so incredibly involved. I was the one who practically ran our neighborhood book club—we read quite a lot of historical fiction, which, as a history teacher, I just absolutely adore, and I would always host and bake scones or something nice. And the school theater planning, too! I used to always help the drama teacher coordinate the period costumes for the spring play, making sure the Victorian dresses were accurate and all of that. 

But lately... I just let it all slide. I haven't hosted or even attended the book club in months, and I haven't been to a single theater planning meeting. Even just simple phone calls to my dearest friends... I will just sit there on the sofa and look at the phone ringing, and I just cannot bring myself to pick it up. I just let all of it slide unless someone really pushes me. My husband practically has to dial the number, hand me the receiver, and stand right there to get me to call my own sister back. It’s not that I don't care about them, it's just that the energy, that natural motivation to participate in my own life, is just... gone. I'm just going through the motions without any of the actual warmth behind it.

symptom_reasoning.S023: The patient describes a profound loss of drive and motivation (avolition), stating she just goes through the motions and lets things slide unless pushed.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient reports no longer participating in previously enjoyed activities like her book club and theater planning, and withdrawing from social contact.
symptom_reasoning.S029: The patient explicitly notes a 'deep, heavy lack of energy' and says her energy to participate in life is 'just... gone.'

turns.doctor_question: Could you tell me approximately how many months or years you have been experiencing these changes in your motivation and social withdrawal?
turns.patient_response:
Well, let me think about that, Dr. Smith. Time just seems to blur together lately, doesn't it? Especially when you are a teacher, you really tend to measure your life in semesters and grading periods rather than actual calendar months. You think in terms of midterms and spring breaks. But if I really sit down and trace it back to when I first started feeling this way... yes, I know exactly when this whole shift began. 

It was right around the time my youngest child left for college. We had spent that entire summer getting him ready, buying all the extra-long twin sheets and shower caddies, you know how it is. And then we drove him up to campus and moved him in. That would make it... well, it has been about a year and two months now. Yes, a year and two months. 

And almost immediately after we came back to our house, that is when I really started to notice this overall change in how I think, how I approach my work, and how I connect with other people. At first, I just chalked it up to the empty nest, you know? It is perfectly natural for a mother to feel a bit adrift when her last baby leaves home. You spend decades where your entire evening revolves around making sure history projects are finished and dinner is on the table at a reasonable hour, and suddenly it is just you and your husband and a painfully quiet house. 

But the feeling just kept dragging on. The fall semester turned into winter, and then spring, and I just never bounced back to my old self. I kept waiting for that natural enthusiasm to return, for the desire to host my book club or help with the school play to just kick back in, but it never did. So yes, it has been a year and two months of just... operating differently in the world, just feeling this heavy shift in my entire routine.

symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient confirms a prolonged loss of enthusiasm and motivation, specifically noting the absence of desire to engage in previously enjoyed social activities like hosting a book club or helping with school plays.
symptom_reasoning.S081: The patient explicitly links the onset of her emotional and behavioral changes to the identifiable stressor of her youngest child leaving for college.

turns.doctor_question: During this past year and two months, have there been any periods where these experiences with the emails and the voice completely stopped, or have they been present consistently the entire time?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, goodness, no, Dr. Smith. I see why you might think that, given how I was just explaining the timeline, but I should be very clear here. The... the heavy feeling, that complete drain of my energy and pulling away from the book club and the theater costumes, that has been going on for the full year and two months since my son moved into his dorm. But these other things? The emails and the voice? That is a much more recent development. 

I mean, if I really sit and think about it... it was right after we came back from the winter holiday break. I was just starting to put together my schedule for the AP European History spring review sessions. Because, you know, the AP exams are in May, and if you don't start reviewing the material in late January, the students simply won't be ready for the Document-Based Questions, which are terribly rigorous and require so much preparation. I was sitting at my dining room table, surrounded by grading rubrics, and it was right around then that I started really noticing the peculiar phrasing in the principal's staff announcements. 

So, if I am being precise, the coded-message worries and... and that voice I sometimes catch myself answering when the house is too quiet... those have only been happening for about four months. 

Yes, four months. It definitely hasn't been the entire year and two months. It's almost as if the exhaustion and the lack of motivation set in first, just dragging on and on through the fall, and then, only in this most recent term, did this whole business with the codes and the voice actually begin. So it has just been these last four months of dealing with that particular, very heavy distraction on top of the empty nest feeling.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient mentions 'coded-message worries' regarding the principal's staff announcements, indicating referential delusions.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient describes hearing a 'voice I sometimes catch myself answering when the house is too quiet,' confirming auditory hallucinations.
symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient describes a 'heavy feeling' and an 'empty nest feeling,' indicating depressed mood and emptiness.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient reports 'pulling away from the book club and the theater costumes' and a 'lack of motivation,' confirming loss of interest and motivation.
symptom_reasoning.S029: The patient mentions a 'complete drain of my energy' and 'exhaustion,' confirming fatigue.

turns.doctor_question: When you are speaking with your colleagues or your husband, have they ever mentioned that they find it difficult to follow your train of thought, or that your speech sometimes doesn't seem to make sense to them?
turns.patient_response:
Well, Dr. Smith, that is an interesting question, because... well, no, not really. I mean, they haven't explicitly said anything like that. I am a teacher, after all, and when you spend your entire professional life standing in front of a classroom of thirty restless teenagers trying to explain the complexities of the French Revolution or the intricacies of the Industrial Revolution, you really have to learn how to speak clearly and keep your thoughts organized. You simply cannot afford to lose your train of thought, or they will completely check out, and getting them back is nearly impossible.

So, when I speak to my husband, or to my colleagues in the staff lounge... I still speak the way I always have. I mean, my husband, David—we've been married for thirty years, and we have our own rhythm of talking, you know? He might notice if I am quieter than usual, or if I don't initiate the conversation, like I was telling you about with the phone calls, but when I do speak, he understands me perfectly fine. We talk about the grocery list, or when the car needs an oil change, or what our son is doing up at college, and it all flows very normally. 

And at school, it's the same thing. I sit in the department meetings, and when it is my turn to give an update on the AP exam prep or discuss the new textbook adoptions, I present my points just as clearly as I always have. The principal—even with those strange emails—has never once pulled me aside to say I was being confusing or that my sentences weren't making sense. I still use my teacher voice, I still outline my thoughts... I suppose the content of what I am thinking about, especially when I am alone in the quiet house, is what feels so different and overwhelming, but the actual physical act of speaking and stringing words together? No, that has remained completely intact. They haven't mentioned anything about me being hard to follow at all.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient explicitly denies that her speech is hard to follow or doesn't make sense, stating she speaks clearly and her thoughts remain organized.

turns.doctor_question: Have there been any times recently where you have felt physically 'stuck' or unable to move, almost as if your body became frozen in a specific position for a period of time?
turns.patient_response:
Well, physically stuck? Like frozen like a statue? No, Dr. Smith, I haven't experienced anything quite like that. My body still moves when I want it to move, I don't just lock up in the middle of the hallway or anything of that sort. But... there have been some other things, some physical things, I suppose you could say, that have been rather bothersome lately. It is actually quite embarrassing, to be completely honest with you, especially given my profession.

You see, when you are a teacher, especially when you are trying to coordinate something complex—like the upcoming spring art fair, for instance, which is always a massive undertaking because we have to coordinate with the fine arts department and ensure all the display boards are perfectly aligned in the gymnasium—you really need to be efficient. You need to keep things moving. But lately... well, during these art fair meetings, or even right in the middle of my AP European History lessons, I will catch myself doing the strangest things. 

I will be right in the middle of a task, perhaps handing out the DBQ rubrics or organizing the art supplies, and I will just... stop. But not frozen, no. I will stop what I am supposed to be doing, and I will start rearranging things. Like the dry-erase markers on the whiteboard tray. I will suddenly feel this intense need to line them up in a very particular pattern—perhaps by color, or by the amount of ink left in them, or just spaced exactly an inch apart. And I will stand there, just shifting the markers back and forth, back and forth, completely ignoring the lesson plan or the meeting agenda. 

And then there are the words. Sometimes, a colleague will ask me a direct question, like, "Susan, did you get the requisition forms for the display boards?" And instead of saying yes or no, I will just... repeat what they said. "Requisition forms for the display boards." Just like that. I don't even realize I am doing it until the words are already out of my mouth. And they will look at me, waiting for an actual answer, and I just feel my face flush with embarrassment because it completely interrupts the flow of what we are supposed to be doing. It is highly unprofessional, and I know it is happening, but in that split second, it is almost like my brain just echoes them instead of generating my own response. So no, I am not frozen, but my actions... they certainly get derailed in these very peculiar, repetitive ways.

symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient denies being physically frozen (stupor/catalepsy) but confirms experiencing echolalia, repeating colleagues' words instead of generating her own response.
symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient describes an intense need to repetitively arrange and line up objects (markers) in a very particular pattern, indicative of ordering and arranging compulsions.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever found yourself completely unable to move or speak for a period of time, even when you were fully aware of what was happening around you?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, no, Dr. Smith, I think perhaps we might be slightly misunderstanding each other. I apologize if I wasn't clear just a moment ago when I was talking about the whiteboard markers. I have never been completely unable to move or speak, like someone in a coma or a trance. I am always fully aware of my surroundings—painfully aware, in fact, which is exactly why the whole situation is so terribly upsetting to me! 

As I was just trying to explain, I don't freeze up. It is more that my actions and my words just get... derailed. For instance, like I said about those art-fair meetings or during my AP lessons, I'll be right in the middle of a task. I might be handing out a stack of graded rubrics, and instead of just passing them down the rows like I have done for thirty years, I will just stop mid-task and start rearranging the papers. I'll become completely preoccupied with making sure the edges of the papers are perfectly flush, or sorting them in a very particular pattern on my podium. My body is moving perfectly fine, you see, but it is doing *that* instead of what it should be doing. 

And it is the exact same thing with my speech. I am never entirely mute or unable to form words. I just... I repeat a phrase from someone else instead of responding normally. If a student asks, "Are we being graded on this?" I might just say, "Are we being graded on this?" right back to them. I am speaking, and I am entirely aware that they are staring at me, waiting for a real, substantive answer, and I just feel this awful flush of embarrassment because I know I am interrupting the very thing I am supposed to be doing. The lesson just grinds to a halt. So, no, I am never completely unable to move or speak, I am just... doing and saying these peculiar, repetitive things at the most inconvenient times.

symptom_reasoning.S022: Although the patient explicitly denies stupor and mutism (being unable to move or speak), they confirm other subtypes of disorganized/abnormal behavior, specifically echolalia (repeating a student's phrase) and stereotyped/manneristic movements (stopping mid-task to rearrange papers in a specific pattern).
